questions.problem: Consider the arc of the curve $y=\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ that lies between the lines $x=0$ and $x=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ What integral gives the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y=f(x),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from $x=0$ to $x=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\sqrt{1+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\sqrt{1+{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the arc of the curve $y=\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}$ that lies in the first quadrant between the line $x=0$ and its $x$-intercept. What integral gives the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y=f(x),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

First, we need to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we find where the curve intersects the $x$-axis by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}} & =0 \\ 4-{x}^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2} & =4 \\ x & =\pm 2\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $x=0$ to $x=2.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}) \\  & =-\frac{x}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}(\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}})\sqrt{1+{(-\frac{x}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}\,\sqrt{1+\frac{{x}^{2}}{4-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}\,\sqrt{\frac{4}{4-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}\cdot \frac{2}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the arc of the curve $y=2-\sqrt{x}$ that lies between the lines $x=0$ and $x=4.$ What integral gives the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y=f(x),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${x}_{1}=0$ to ${x}_{2}=4.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2-\sqrt{x})=-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{4}(2-\sqrt{x})\sqrt{1+{(-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{4}(2-\sqrt{x})\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{4x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{4}(2-\sqrt{x})\sqrt{\frac{4x+1}{x}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y=f(x),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

First, we need to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we find where the curve intersects the $x$-axis by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}1-(x+1)^{2} & =0 \\ (x+1)^{2} & =1 \\ x+1 & =\pm 1 \\ x & =-1\pm 1 \\ x & =-2,0\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $x=-2$ to $x=0.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1-(x+1)^{2})=-2x-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-2}^{0}(1-(x+1)^{2})\sqrt{1+(-2x-2)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-2}^{0}(-{x}^{2}-2x)\sqrt{4{x}^{2}+8x+5}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y=f(x),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{3}$ to ${x}_{2}=1.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\sqrt{3x+1})=\frac{3}{2\sqrt{3x+1}}\,⇒\,{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}=\frac{9}{4(3x+1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-1/3}^{1}\sqrt{3x+1}\sqrt{1+\frac{9}{4(3x+1)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-1/3}^{1}\sqrt{3x+1}\sqrt{\frac{12x+13}{4(3x+1)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-1/3}^{1}\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{12x+13}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1/3}^{1}\sqrt{12x+13}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi \cdot \frac{(12x+13)^{3/2}}{18}\,{|}_{-1/3}^{1} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{18}({25}^{3/2}-{9}^{3/2}) \\  & =\frac{49\pi }{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the arc of the curve $x=\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}-1$ that lies between the lines $y=0$ and $y=1.$ Calculate the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $x=f(y),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${y}_{1}=0$ to ${y}_{2}=1.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}-1)=y\,⇒\,{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}={y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}y\sqrt{1+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the substitution 

$$
u={y}^{2}+1\,⇒\,(\frac{1}{2})\text{d}u=y\,\text{d}y,
$$

we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}y\sqrt{1+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}\sqrt{u}\,(\frac{1}{2})\text{d}u \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\pi {\frac{2\sqrt{{u}^{3}}}{3}\,|}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2\pi }{3}(\sqrt{{2}^{3}}-\sqrt{{1}^{3}}) \\  & =\frac{2\pi }{3}(2\sqrt{2}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y=f(x),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${x}_{1}=0$ to ${x}_{2}=1.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2x+1)=2\,⇒\,{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(2x+1)\sqrt{1+4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(2x+1)\sqrt{5}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi \sqrt{5}{\int }_{0}^{1}(2x+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi \sqrt{5}({x}^{2}+x){|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =2\pi \sqrt{5}((1+1)-0) \\  & =4\pi \sqrt{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the arc of the curve $x=\sqrt{9-{y}^{2}}$ that lies between the lines $y=0$ and $y=2.$ Calculate the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $x=f(y),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${y}_{1}=0$ to ${y}_{2}=2.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\sqrt{9-{y}^{2}})=-\frac{y}{\sqrt{9-{y}^{2}}}\,⇒\,{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}=\frac{{y}^{2}}{9-{y}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}y\sqrt{1+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9-{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}y\sqrt{\frac{9}{9-{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}\,\frac{3y}{\sqrt{9-{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =3\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{2y}{\sqrt{9-{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the substitution 

$$
u=9-{y}^{2}\,⇒\,\text{d}u=-2y\,\text{d}y,
$$

we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =3\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{2y}{\sqrt{9-{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =-3\pi {\int }_{9}^{5}{u}^{-1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\pi {\int }_{5}^{9}{u}^{-1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\pi {[2\sqrt{u}\,]}_{5}^{9} \\  & =6\pi (3-\sqrt{5}).\end{aligned}
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${y}_{1}=0$ to ${y}_{2}=2.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\frac{4}{3}{y}^{3/2})=2\sqrt{y}\,⇒\,{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}=4y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}y\sqrt{1+4y}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the substitution 

$$
u=1+4y\,⇒\,\frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}u=\text{d}y,\,y=\frac{u-1}{4},
$$

we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}y\sqrt{1+4y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{9}\frac{u-1}{4}\sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{8}{\int }_{1}^{9}(u-1)\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{8}{\int }_{1}^{9}({u}^{3/2}-{u}^{1/2})\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{8}(\frac{2}{5}{u}^{5/2}-\frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2})\,{|}_{1}^{9} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{8}((\frac{2}{5}\cdot {9}^{5/2}-\frac{2}{3}\cdot {9}^{3/2})-(\frac{2}{5}\cdot {1}^{5/2}-\frac{2}{3}\cdot {1}^{3/2})) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{8}((\frac{2}{5}\cdot 243-\frac{2}{3}\cdot 27)-(\frac{2}{5}-\frac{2}{3})) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{8}(\frac{396}{5}+\frac{4}{15}) \\  & =\frac{149\pi }{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S = \int 2\pi y\,\textrm d s.
$$

$$
\textrm d s = \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}\right)^2}\,\textrm d x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S = 2\pi \int_{x_1}^{x_2} y \sqrt{1+ \left( \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \right)^2} \: \textrm{d}x.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from $x_1=0$ to $x_2={2}.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({e}^{x})={e}^{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{e}^{x}\sqrt{1+({e}^{x})^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{e}^{x}\sqrt{1+{e}^{2x}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the arc of the curve $x=y^3-y$ that lies in the second quadrant between its $y$-intercepts. What integral gives the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis?

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14082610/assets/1bdbe21cbb517645dfe9362f3313c2d85118acfea1d839fe33ae9b9ac6c3ed50.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S = \int 2\pi y\,\textrm d s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $x = f(y),$ we have 

$$
\textrm d s = \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d y}\right)^2}\,\textrm d y.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S = 2\pi \int_{y_1}^{y_2} y \sqrt{1+ \left( \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} \right)^2} \: \textrm{d}y.
$$

First, we need to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we find where the curve intersects the $y$-axis by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{3}-y & =0 \\ y({y}^{2}-1) & =0 \\ y & =0,\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $y=0$ to $y=1.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{3}-y)=3{y}^{2}-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}y\sqrt{1+{(3{y}^{2}-1)}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}y\sqrt{2-6{y}^{2}+9{y}^{4}}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Consider the arc of the curve $y=\sqrt{x-2}$ that lies between the lines $x=2$ and $x=4.$ Calculate the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S = \int 2\pi y\,\textrm d s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y = f(x),$ we have 

$$
\textrm d s = \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}\right)^2}\,\textrm d x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S = 2\pi \int_{x_1}^{x_2} y \sqrt{1+ \left( \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \right)^2} \: \textrm{d}x.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from $x_1=2$ to $x_2=4.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\sqrt{x-2})=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x-2}}\,⇒\,{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}=\frac{1}{4(x-2)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{2}^{4}\sqrt{x-2}\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{4(x-2)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{2}^{4}\sqrt{x-2}\sqrt{\frac{4x-7}{4(x-2)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{2}^{4}\sqrt{x-2}(\frac{\sqrt{4x-7}}{2\sqrt{x-2}})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{2}^{4}\sqrt{4x-7}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the substitution 

$$
u=4x-7 \quad \Rightarrow\quad \textrm du = 4\,\textrm dx,
$$

we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =\pi {\int }_{2}^{4}\sqrt{4x-7}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}{\int }_{1}^{9}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\cdot \frac{2}{3}{\sqrt{{u}^{3}}\,|}_{1}^{9} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}(27-1) \\  & =\frac{13\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$
